chunks.title: This Website: Architecture & Tech
chunks.tags: site website portfolio how built made technology stack architecture special unique framework vanilla javascript html css
chunks.content: Built with Claude Code (main features) and OpenCode (maintenance). Each page is a standalone HTML file with vanilla JavaScript, a shared CSS design system (Deep Sea Terminal theme), and Google Fonts. The pages are served as static files on GitHub Pages. The homepage fish canvas is a layered steering system. An eight-level behavior priority stack runs edge avoidance, heading commitment, state behaviors, collision, schooling, and wander in order. Three size classes each behave differently. Schooling runs in V-formation with stable slot assignment. A breadth-first navigation field routes fish around drawn walls. The design page runs the same engine under a blueprint canvas that recognizes drawn shapes and turns them into walls and obstacles. Search is three tiers over a precomputed index. Tier one is BM25 keyword retrieval with field boosting. Tier two adds all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings quantized to int8, fused with the keyword results by reciprocal rank. Tier three is optional generation, in-browser through WebGPU or against a local LMStudio or Ollama endpoint. Results render as one adaptive surface whose density follows how specific the query was. Other features: shape-based geometric navigation, an infinite-canvas playground with pan and zoom, and a cosmos starfield on the art page. A search overlay opens on every page via Cmd-K.
chunks.micro: Static HTML per page, vanilla JS, built with Claude Code.
chunks.tldr: Standalone HTML and vanilla JS on GitHub Pages, with a layered fish steering system, a shape-recognition canvas, and a three-tier search.

chunks.content: The homepage hero is an interactive aquatic ecosystem. Draw shapes on the canvas to spawn entities. Loops become fish, small, medium or large based on size. Squares become coral, triangles become jellyfish, circles become bubbles, and taps drop food pellets. Fish have layered autonomous behaviors including edge avoidance, schooling formations, territorial challenges, predator fleeing, and coral homecoming. Press D for debug view. Touch and mouse supported.

chunks.title: AI Search System
chunks.tags: search AI LLM qwen webgpu lmstudio ollama minisearch bm25 browser local model inference
chunks.content: Three-tier search with progressive enhancement. Tier 1: MiniSearch BM25 instant keyword search, always on. Tier 2: LFM2.5-350M running in-browser via WebGPU and Transformers.js. Tier 3: local LMStudio or Ollama models, detected when the visitor clicks Detect, for higher quality answers. Also supports custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Engine color coding: WebGPU blue, LMStudio purple, Ollama orange, Custom green. AI can be toggled on or off by the user.
chunks.micro: BM25 → WebGPU Qwen → your local model.
chunks.tldr: Three tiers: instant BM25, in-browser LFM2.5-350M, and local LMStudio or Ollama on request, all user-toggleable.

chunks.title: JHDesign Review Canvas: Design Review Tooling
chunks.tags: review canvas tooling design review iframe grid focus git multiplayer collaborative ratings comments annotation openprose internal tool built
chunks.content: The JHDesign Review Canvas is a tool John built to review dozens of live website experiments at once. It shows the contents of a repo as one navigable page with three view modes: canvas, grid and focus. Every page is a live iframe with star ratings, typed comments, and freehand drawings composited onto screenshots. Review state lives in git and each reviewer writes only their own file. Feedback merges cleanly, and a GitHub repo is all it takes to collaborate. A display cut of it is embedded at the end of the OpenProse case study.

chunks.title: Handling Disagreement
chunks.tags: disagreement disagreed disagree conflict pushback overruled convinced advocacy stakeholders engineering compromise authority product decisions collaboration
chunks.content: Does the best design available at the level of authority he has, and advocates for what he thinks is best for the product. Works with engineering to think through ways to make a thing easier to build while still getting what the user needs. Treats compromise as a forcing function: simplifying down to the core requirement is often where the innovation shows up. Exhausts the options first, then defers on the genuinely impossible.
chunks.micro: Advocate hard, then defer to the impossible.
chunks.tldr: Does the best design available at his level of authority and treats compromise as a forcing function toward the core requirement.

chunks.title: Ambiguity and Constraint
chunks.tags: ambiguity structure standards scoping constraints timeline cuts prioritization process design thinking
chunks.content: Ambiguity is where he works best. He is always looking for structure, including the unspoken structure inside processes everyone already considers settled. He generates standards as they are needed. He deliberately revisits ambiguity after a project has been iterated into a narrow scope, to keep in mind that everything could still change. That pays off when a timeline is cut in half. He usually already knows what will have to go before anyone asks, and can keep paring if it halves again.
chunks.micro: Thrives in ambiguity. Knows what goes first.
chunks.tldr: Looks for structure everywhere, including the unspoken kind inside settled processes, and keeps ambiguity live on tightly scoped work.

chunks.title: Critique and Design Reviews
chunks.tags: critique design review feedback how might we solutionizing stakeholders roast facilitation shared understanding
chunks.content: Runs critique playfully, leaning on open-ended "how might we" statements to avoid solutionizing, where a design gets taken too literally too early. Sets expectations going into any review, manages stakeholders, and levels with peers. Keeps the work outside himself. Any given iteration is the best current approach, so he holds it loosely and enjoys a good roast. The best products stand up to scrutiny, so he invites it. He invites people to see the potential while giving concrete answers. He guides the room from yes or no toward shared understanding, so the best outcome emerges from critique as a process.
chunks.micro: Invite the roast. Hold the work loosely.
chunks.tldr: Runs critique playfully and open-ended, steering the room toward shared understanding so the outcome emerges from the process.

chunks.title: Research That Changed the Design: Nanome
chunks.tags: user research usability testing qualitative coding pharmaceutical scientists VR navigation spotlight follow teleportation pivot evidence
chunks.content: On Nanome 2 he designed the test criteria and ran multiple rounds of usability testing with real pharmaceutical user groups. Testers included existing Nanome 1 users and new ones. To make sense of feedback from scientists with different backgrounds he used qualitative data coding. Responses sorted into actionable bugs, "how might we" explorations, evidence supporting features, and usability patterns, so the team could prioritize. The first rounds confirmed the new aesthetic was appreciated but showed VR navigation was still hard. One tester: "Still have trouble with moving around the structure and other users." He led a pivot, removing teleportation-based navigation and introducing the Spotlight/Follow paradigm. It is a non-rivalrous approach adapted from 2D tools into XR, letting collaborators share focus while exploring independently. It became one of Nanome 2 signature features.
chunks.micro: Testing killed teleportation. Spotlight/Follow replaced it.
chunks.tldr: Multi-round testing with pharma users, coded qualitatively, produced a navigation pivot that became one of Nanome 2’s signature features.

chunks.title: Working with AI
chunks.tags: AI agentic design practice claude code verification QA steering vibe coding prototyping workflow definitions expectations
chunks.content: Treats AI as an omni-developer that is a bit too obedient, which makes clear definitions and expectations the designer’s job. Builds systems to verify output. Sees AI as a middle zone between direct hand manipulation, like drawing and Figma, and passive vibe coding, and prefers intentional steering. Coming from a decade-long design career, the practice inverted. He used to build a design up from reference and pastiche toward the requirements. He now generates candidates that already meet the requirements and pares them down, closer to sculpting than painting. QA stays manual, and he holds that line. He has always held that a designer should know every screen and every state. That matters more now that AI can build so much so fast. So go and test it.
chunks.micro: An omni-developer that is a bit too obedient.
chunks.tldr: Treats AI as an omni-developer that needs definitions, expectations and verification systems, steered deliberately.

chunks.title: Failure and Resilience
chunks.tags: failure resilience avatarmedic pivot funding startup lifeguard rescue perspective lessons consultancy
chunks.content: AvatarMEDIC was ambitious and too early, underfunded, and eventually his own capital was exhausted. He gave up the fundraising product dream and pivoted the company into a consultancy that brought in revenue. He holds that failures are the lead of golden wisdom: transmuting the lesson is what makes a person more resilient. His first job was lifeguarding, dealing with life and death directly. He has saved lives, including being first on scene for a c-spine injury and working large surf rescues. Preventative work makes up most of the job. That gives him a gradient of failure uncommon in tech. Life or death is the only real failure, and as long as you are breathing you can try again.
chunks.micro: Life or death is the only real failure.
chunks.tldr: AvatarMEDIC was too early and underfunded, so he pivoted it into a revenue-earning consultancy.

chunks.title: Harness vs Ecosystem: a brittle metaphor
chunks.tags: philosophy agents orchestration harness ecosystem metaphor guardrails control feedback loops how he thinks
chunks.content: From the orchestration essay: if you think 'harness' you build pipelines, guardrails and kill switches, and control flows one way. If you think 'ecosystem' you build niches, feedback loops and adaptive boundaries, and coordination is mutual. Bad metaphors produce bad systems. The field needs better metaphors before it needs better code. Every negative prompt contains the thing it forbids. Control and danger travel in the same channel, so the harness is self-defeating.
chunks.micro: Harness → pipelines and kill switches. Ecosystem → niches and feedback loops.
chunks.tldr: John's core stance on agents: think ecosystem, because the field needs better metaphors before better code.

chunks.title: The RLM Ratchet
chunks.tags: philosophy agents orchestration ratchet loop learning wasted cycles retry recursion RLM change log how he thinks
chunks.content: From the orchestration essay: agents that loop attempt, fail, retry the same approach, and burn tokens. Evolution ratchets: each cycle preserves what was learned. John's 'RLM ratchet': the model's output becomes its own input, a recursive self-modification where each cycle's delta is the ratchet tooth. Compress what was learned and carry forward only the change log. Coordination then scales O(log n).
chunks.micro: Evolution ratchets: each cycle keeps what was learned.
chunks.tldr: John on wasted agent cycles: ratchet, keeping each cycle's delta and carrying only the change log forward.

chunks.title: Stigmergy: Coordination Through the Environment
chunks.tags: philosophy agents orchestration stigmergy ants pheromone trails swarm intelligence git history test results workspace how he thinks
chunks.content: From the orchestration essay: ants find the shortest path by leaving pheromone traces. Bad paths fade, good paths get reinforced. That is stigmergy: coordination through environmental signals. Applied to agents: test results are fitness signals, git history is a trail of decisions, and the workspace is terrain. Each agent's output reshapes the environment for the next.
chunks.micro: Coordinate through the environment, like ants.
chunks.tldr: John's stigmergy principle: agents coordinate through the workspace, tests and git history, leaving trails.

chunks.title: Fractal Delegation
chunks.tags: philosophy agents orchestration fractal self-similar recursive coordination scale delegation subtasks O(log n) how he thinks
chunks.content: From the orchestration essay: the coordination pattern that works for 3 agents should work for 30 and for 300. Self-similar decomposition: subtasks have the same structure as the parent task. The coordinator–agent relationship is the same at every level. Recovery has the same shape at micro and macro scale. Fractal architectures bound coordination overhead to O(log n), because each level coordinates only its children.
chunks.micro: Same pattern at 3, 30 and 300 agents.
chunks.tldr: John's fractal principle: delegate self-similarly so each level coordinates only its children, at O(log n).

chunks.title: Attractor Basins
chunks.tags: philosophy agents orchestration strange attractor basin dynamical systems self-organize acceptable states robust perturbation how he thinks
chunks.content: From the orchestration essay: define the attractor basin, the set of acceptable states, and let agents self-organize toward coherent behavior. Attractors emerge from simple rules interacting. The system is robust to perturbation: push it and it returns to the basin. It is sensitive to initial conditions, which makes the butterfly effect a feature for exploration.
chunks.micro: Define the basin of acceptable states.
chunks.tldr: John on planning agents: specify the set of acceptable states and let behavior self-organize.

chunks.title: Polychronic Agents: the Temporal Mismatch
chunks.tags: philosophy agents orchestration temporal mismatch timescales clocks polychronic async planning execution feedback circadian how he thinks
chunks.content: From the orchestration essay: agents operate at different timescales. Planning is slow and deliberative, execution fast and procedural, feedback delayed and partial. Pipeline orchestration forces synchronous handoffs between asynchronous processes, so the planner waits and the executor is stuck mid-stride. Most frameworks enforce a single clock. Intelligent systems are polychronic. The body runs many clocks: circadian rhythms, reflex arcs and immune response are coordinated hierarchically across timescales.
chunks.micro: Intelligent systems run many clocks at once.
chunks.tldr: John on why pipelines stall: agents are polychronic, and a single enforced clock mistimes every handoff.

chunks.title: The Living System: Roles Are Discovered
chunks.tags: philosophy agents orchestration ecosystem roles niche plants pollinators predators decomposers keystone learning loop recursion how he thinks
chunks.content: From the orchestration essay's closing picture: an agent ecosystem as a forest floor. Plants are interfaces with persistent roots. Pollinators are message-passing agents. Predators are selection pressure that removes the redundant and enforces quality. Decomposers recycle spent context. Microbes are logging and heartbeats, invisible and essential. The keystone is the agent whose removal collapses the system. Roles are discovered: an organism finds its niche. Each turn of the learning loop is recursion, and the agent IS the loop.
chunks.micro: Every role is a niche an agent finds.
chunks.tldr: John's ecosystem model for agents: interfaces, messengers, selection pressure, recyclers and a keystone, each finding its niche.

chunks.title: READI: Emergency Resource Allocation
chunks.tags: readi teamreadi teamready dashboard emergency resource allocation san diego map at-risk households resource sites food water medical road live product civic
chunks.content: READI (teamreadi.xyz) is a live neighborhood emergency-resource-allocation dashboard for San Diego. It maps at-risk areas, households and resource sites, with food, road, medical and water outputs over 24, 48 and 72-hour horizons. Layers cover risk, transfers, damage (impassable roads), community pings (needs help / can help) and salvageable plants. A live stack shows incoming reports. Actions are broadcast, receive and self-report.

chunks.tldr: READI at teamreadi.xyz is a live map-based dashboard allocating food, water, medical and road resources across San Diego neighborhoods.
